title: Exercise 7A · Q9(b)
summary: Find AC first, halve it to get CD, then find BD in ΔBCD.
alt: Exercise 7A · Q9(b): In the figure, AB = 41 cm, BC = 9 cm, ∠C = 90° and D is the midpoint of AC. Find the value of b, the length of BD.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In the figure, **AB = 41 cm**, **BC = 9 cm** and **∠C = 90°**. **D** is the midpoint of **AC** (the tick marks). We have to find **b**, the length of **BD**.

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔABC, **∠C = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **AB**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AB^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ \role{legB}{AC^2} &= \role{hyp}{AB^2} - \role{legA}{BC^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AB^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ \role{legB}{AC^2} &= \role{hyp}{AB^2} - \role{legA}{BC^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{41^2} - \role{legA}{9^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1681} - \role{legA}{81} \\ &= \role{legB}{1600}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: Take the square root of both sides (a length is positive).\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{AB^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{AC^2} \\ \role{legB}{AC^2} &= \role{hyp}{AB^2} - \role{legA}{BC^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{41^2} - \role{legA}{9^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1681} - \role{legA}{81} \\ &= \role{legB}{1600} \\ \role{legB}{AC} &= \sqrt{1600} = 40\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Use the midpoint
steps.narration: D is the **midpoint** of AC, so **CD is half of AC**.\[\begin{aligned}CD &= \frac{40}{2} \\ &= 20\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔBCD, **∠C = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **BD**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{BD^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{CD^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and add
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and add.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{BD^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{CD^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{9^2} + \role{legB}{20^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{81} + \role{legB}{400} \\ &= \role{hyp}{481}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 481 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{BD^2} &= \role{legA}{BC^2} + \role{legB}{CD^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{9^2} + \role{legB}{20^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{81} + \role{legB}{400} \\ &= \role{hyp}{481} \\ \role{hyp}{BD} &= \sqrt{481} = \role{ans}{21.9\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Check CD
challenges.prompt: AC = 40 cm and D is its midpoint. How long is **CD**?

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.

notes.title: Rounding
notes.text: If the answer is not a whole number, give it to **3 significant figures** unless the question says otherwise.
